explanations.explanation: Honor it is. The verse says, "Like snow in summer and rain at harvest, honor does not befit a fool." Snow in summer and rain at harvest both show up where they don't belong, and so does honor on a fool. If I opened my bakery door in July and found a snowman waiting in line, I'd have questions.

Nice guess, friend, but hard work isn't what the verse puts next to snow in summer. It says, "…honor does not befit a fool." Honor is the thing that's out of place, like rain at harvest. Hard work never even gets invited to this proverb.

A quiet home sounds lovely, but it's not in this verse. The proverb says, "Like snow in summer and rain at harvest, honor does not befit a fool." So the mismatch is honor sitting on a fool. Snow in summer and rain at harvest are just the pictures that go with it.

Careful, friend, because the verse says the opposite. It says an undeserved curse "does not come to rest." The picture is a fluttering sparrow or a darting swallow, birds that keep moving. So that curse never lands. I'd say that's good news for anybody on the receiving end.

False is right, friend. The verse says, "Like a fluttering sparrow or darting swallow, an undeserved curse does not come to rest." Try getting a swallow to sit still on your counter. It's not happening, and neither is the curse landing. I know because I watched birds from a kitchen window, not a drawer.

explanations.answer: Or you'll end up like him
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The verse says, "Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you yourself will be like him." Match his folly and now there are two of you doing it. Two people arguing nonsense in a kitchen is just a louder kitchen.

I get why you'd think so, but the verse doesn't say that. It says, "Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you yourself will be like him." The warning is about what happens to you. Answer him in his folly and you end up like him.

Close to a real-life worry, friend, but the verse doesn't go there. It says, "Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you yourself will be like him." The danger it names is becoming like him. Nothing about him turning on you.

explanations.answer: So he won't be wise in his own eyes
explanations.explanation: Yes! The verse says, "Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he become wise in his own eyes." Yes, it sits right after the line that says don't answer him that way. Two lines, side by side, and the text doesn't stop to explain how they fit together. I'm just gonna stand here with my mustache scratching my chin.

explanations.answer: So he'll leave you alone for good
explanations.explanation: That would be nice, friend, but the verse doesn't promise it. It says, "Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he become wise in his own eyes." The reason given is about how the fool sees himself. Nothing about him leaving anybody alone.

explanations.answer: So other people won't follow him
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, but the verse never mentions followers. It says, "Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he become wise in his own eyes." The reason is that he doesn't become wise in his own eyes. That's the whole reason the proverb gives.

True! The verse says, "Like cutting off one's own feet or drinking violence is the sending of a message by the hand of a fool." Cutting off your own feet, and then asking someone to carry the message for you. Friend, that's one expensive way to send a note.

It's actually true, friend. The verse says, "Like cutting off one's own feet or drinking violence is the sending of a message by the hand of a fool." Cutting off your own feet is one of the two pictures it uses. The other one is drinking violence. Neither one sounds like a good day.

Proverb is it. The verse says, "Like lame legs hanging limp is a proverb in the mouth of a fool." Legs hanging limp can't carry anybody anywhere. A wise saying in a fool's mouth is like that, with no strength behind it.
A promise is a fair guess, friend, but that's not the word here. The verse says, "Like lame legs hanging limp is a proverb in the mouth of a fool." The proverb itself is what hangs limp in his mouth.

A secret in the wrong mouth does cause trouble, but this verse isn't about that. It says, "Like lame legs hanging limp is a proverb in the mouth of a fool." The word is proverb. Limp legs, limp proverb.

explanations.answer: The one who hires a fool or passerby
explanations.explanation: That's right. The verse says, "Like an archer who wounds at random is he who hires a fool or passerby." An archer shooting at random can hit anybody. Hiring somebody off the street without knowing them is that kind of shot.

explanations.answer: The one who trusts a fool's advice
explanations.explanation: Trusting a fool's advice sounds like it belongs, friend, but the verse says something different. It says, "Like an archer who wounds at random is he who hires a fool or passerby." So the picture is about the one doing the hiring.

explanations.answer: The one who walks along with fools
explanations.explanation: Walking along with fools is a different proverb for a different day. This verse says, "Like an archer who wounds at random is he who hires a fool or passerby." So it's the hiring that's compared to the random arrow.

Repeats, yes. The verse says, "As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly." It's a rough picture, and the proverb meant it to be. He keeps going back to the same mistake. I once reached for the same hot pan twice in one morning, so I'm not judging.

Hiding would at least show some shame, friend, but the verse doesn't say it. It says, "As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly." The dog goes right back, and the fool does the same thing again. Nobody's hiding anything.

Regret would be a step in the right direction, but that's not the word. The verse says, "As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly." The fool goes back and does it again. The text says nothing about him feeling sorry.

Careful, friend, because it's the other way around. The verse asks, "Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes?" Then it says, "There is more hope for a fool than for him." So the fool has more hope than the man who thinks he's already wise.

False is right. The verse says, "Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him." Somebody who thinks he's already got it all figured out is hard to teach. I'd rather be a fool with an open mind and a warm oven.

explanations.answer: A lion is in the road
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The slacker says, "A lion is in the road! A fierce lion roams the public square!" It's a big, scary announcement, and it happens to be a great reason to stay inside. I think we've all had a reason like that on a Monday morning.
A storm would be a fine excuse, but it's not the slacker's. He says, "A lion is in the road! A fierce lion roams the public square!" The slacker's excuse has teeth.
Robbers would scare me too, friend, but they're not in this verse. The slacker says, "A lion is in the road! A fierce lion roams the public square!" The danger he names is a lion.

Bed is the word. The verse says, "As a door turns on its hinges, so the slacker turns on his bed." A door swings back and forth and stays right where it's attached. The slacker rolls over and goes nowhere either.

Turning on your heel means you're going somewhere, friend, and this slacker isn't. The verse says, "As a door turns on its hinges, so the slacker turns on his bed." He's flipping over in bed. A door like that never leaves the doorframe.

Turning on your word is a real thing people do, but that's not this verse. It says, "As a door turns on its hinges, so the slacker turns on his bed." The slacker stays put in bed and just rolls around.

Not quite, friend, it's the opposite. The verse says, "The slacker buries his hand in the dish; it wearies him to bring it back to his mouth." He's not eating fast. He's too worn out to even lift his hand back up.

False is right. The verse says, "The slacker buries his hand in the dish; it wearies him to bring it back to his mouth." His hand is in the dish, but lifting it is the hard part. Nobody's empty-dish champion here.

explanations.answer: Wiser than seven men who answer discreetly
explanations.explanation: You got it. The verse says, "The slacker is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who answer discreetly." He can barely lift his hand, and he still thinks he outsmarts seven careful men. That's a whole lot of confidence for somebody lying down.

explanations.answer: Wiser than all of the king's advisers
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a big claim, friend, but it's not what the verse says. It says, "The slacker is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who answer discreetly." The number is seven, and they're men who answer carefully.

explanations.answer: Wiser than the elders at the city gate
explanations.explanation: The elders and the city gate don't show up in this verse. It says, "The slacker is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who answer discreetly." So he's measuring himself against seven discreet men.

A dog, yes. The verse says, "Like one who grabs a dog by the ears is a passerby who meddles in a quarrel not his own." Grabbing a dog by the ears is a quick way to get yourself in the middle of something. Same goes for walking into an argument that isn't yours.

A wolf would make this a scarier proverb, friend, but the verse says dog. It says, "Like one who grabs a dog by the ears is a passerby who meddles in a quarrel not his own." An ordinary dog is bad enough to grab by the ears.
A bear is a dramatic guess, and I respect the drama. But the verse says, "Like one who grabs a dog by the ears is a passerby who meddles in a quarrel not his own." It's a dog. No bears in this one.

True! The verse says, "Like a madman shooting firebrands and deadly arrows, so is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, 'I was only joking!'" Calling it a joke afterward doesn't un-shoot the arrows. A joke that burns somebody isn't a joke.

It's actually true, friend. The verse says, "Like a madman shooting firebrands and deadly arrows, so is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, 'I was only joking!'" The two pictures go together in the same sentence. Nobody gets to say sorry-just-kidding after the arrows fly.
Wood goes in the first blank. The verse says, "Without wood, a fire goes out…" No wood, no fire. My ovens agree with that one.
Gossip goes in the second blank. The verse says, "…without gossip, a conflict ceases." A fight needs something to feed on, and gossip is that something. Take it away and the conflict stops.

Water seems like the obvious fire word, friend, but it's not in this verse. The verse says, "Without wood, a fire goes out…" The word it uses is wood, and the proverb is about what keeps a fire going.

Music is a lovely thing, but this verse doesn't use it. It says, "Without wood, a fire goes out; without gossip, a conflict ceases." Wood and gossip are the two words. Music can stay in the bakery with me.

Silver isn't anywhere near this verse, friend. It says, "Without wood, a fire goes out; without gossip, a conflict ceases." Both blanks are about what keeps something burning. Wood feeds the fire, and gossip feeds the conflict.
Yes, down deep. The verse says, "The words of a gossip are like choice morsels that go down into the inmost being." They go down easy and settle in deep. That's why they're hard to forget.

explanations.answer: Out of the mouth and away
explanations.explanation: That would be handy, friend, but it's not what the verse says. It says the words are "like choice morsels that go down into the inmost being." They don't float away. They sink in.
The city gates don't come up in this verse. It says the words of a gossip are "like choice morsels that go down into the inmost being." The direction is down, not up.

That's not quite it, friend. The verse says, "Like glaze covering an earthen vessel are burning lips and a wicked heart." The glaze is compared to burning lips and a wicked heart, not to a wise man's kind words. A shiny finish on the outside, and something else inside.

False is right. The verse says, "Like glaze covering an earthen vessel are burning lips and a wicked heart." It's not a wise man's kind words. It's burning lips and a wicked heart, shiny on the outside like glaze on a clay pot.

Exactly. The verse says, "When he speaks graciously, do not believe him, for seven abominations fill his heart." Nice words on the outside don't tell you what's in the heart. I'd keep my oven mitts on around that one.

Gentle is a good instinct, friend, but that's not what this verse says. It says, "When he speaks graciously, do not believe him, for seven abominations fill his heart." The instruction is not to believe him.

Looking out for your neighbors is kind, but the verse doesn't say it. It says, "When he speaks graciously, do not believe him, for seven abominations fill his heart." What you're told to do is not believe him.
Not so, friend. The verse says, "Though his hatred is concealed by deception, his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly." He may hide it for a while, but it comes out. The hiding doesn't last.

False is right. The verse says, "Though his hatred is concealed by deception, his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly." It's hidden for now, but it won't stay that way. Even the best disguise doesn't last forever.
That's right. The verse says, "He who digs a pit will fall into it…" The hole he dug for somebody else catches him instead. Dig carefully, friend.

explanations.answer: He's made to fill it in
explanations.explanation: Filling it in would be a fair punishment, friend, but the verse says something else. It says, "He who digs a pit will fall into it…" He doesn't fill it. He lands in it.
No guards in this one, friend. The verse says, "He who digs a pit will fall into it…" The pit itself takes care of it. He ends up in the hole he dug.

True. The last verse says, "A lying tongue hates those it crushes, and a flattering mouth causes ruin." Sweet-talk can ruin things just like lies can. We've come a long way from snow in summer, friend, and you stuck with it.

It's actually true, friend. The chapter ends with, "A lying tongue hates those it crushes, and a flattering mouth causes ruin." Flattery may sound pleasant, but the verse says it causes ruin. That's a sweet-looking cookie with a bad surprise inside.
